draft.title: An author's style
card: Style is the way an author typically writes. It is the pattern in their choices, so it shows across a text or across several texts.

Style comes from choices of words (plain or fancy, formal or casual), sentence lengths (short and sharp or long and flowing), devices (such as simile or repetition) and structure (how the text is ordered).
Example: an author who often uses short sentences, simple words and sudden endings to scenes has a blunt, fast style.
To describe a style, look for what an author does again and again, then say how it affects a reader. One odd choice does not make a style.
draft.remember: Style is the pattern in an author's choices, and it creates a particular effect on the reader.

a.q: Which of these best describes an author's style?
opts: The pattern in their choices of words, sentences and devices
The topic that they write about in one particular book
The order in which their books were published
The opinion that a reader forms about the author
a.why: Style is the way an author typically writes, shown in repeated choices. A topic is what a text is about, not how it is written, so it is not style.
a.clue: Style is about how an author writes, not what happens.

b.q: Zara reads three stories by one author. Each has long, flowing sentences, rich descriptions and slow openings. Which statement about the author's style is best?
opts: The author has a style that is slow and detailed
The author has no style, as the stories differ
The author uses only long sentences in every text
The author has a style because the stories are long
b.why: The same choices appear in all three stories, so they form a pattern, and that pattern is a slow, detailed style. Length of a story is not a choice of words, sentences or devices, so it does not show style.
b.clue: Look for what the three stories share in how they are written.

a.best: The pattern in their choices of words, sentences and devices

b.best: The author has a style that is slow and detailed
